generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, any subject gives you plenty to revise actively across all three families. A visual map can link an idea to the evidence for and against it; reading an argument aloud exposes the gaps in it; and walking through the steps of a process anchors their order. The strongest revision combines families, because material you can both diagram and explain aloud is material you can retrieve under pressure.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students revising the same difficult topic, one with several linked parts that are easily confused.

Student A makes one neat set of written notes and reads them over each day. The notes are accurate and tidy, but they never leave a single family: it is all reading. The parts blur together, because nothing forces the topic to be reproduced or spoken aloud. One passive technique, however often it is repeated, is still passive.

Student B draws the topic as a labelled diagram, then explains each part aloud into a recording. They then lay a card for each part around the desk and rehearse how the parts connect while moving between them. Three techniques from three families, each demanding a different kind of production. The diagram fixes the structure, the spoken version catches the gaps, and the layout anchors how the parts relate. This is a varied, active approach.

Both revised the topic for the same time. Student B chose techniques across families that matched the material, and finished with knowledge that could be retrieved by more than one route.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision techniques fall into three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. You can now tell them apart and say what each is suited to, judge which turn a passive task active, and select a mix across families for a topic. What unites the strong choices is production: rebuilding, explaining or enacting the material rather than merely reviewing it. The final lesson takes your prepared knowledge into the exam itself.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's revision more active than Student A's?

items.text: Student B used techniques from several families, each forcing the material to be produced in a different way.
Student B made neater and more accurate notes than Student A.
Student B spent longer revising than Student A.
Student B read a single set of notes more often.

feedback.correct: That's right. Drawing on several families, each demanding production, is what made it active.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about producing the material across more than one family.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B used techniques from several families, each forcing a different kind of production. Neater notes, more time or more rereading would all have stayed passive.
